analysis.one_liner: Requires wealthy colleges to cover part of students' costs and pay for loan defaults.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in August 2022 with no cosponsors, sat in the Senate education committee, and died when the Congress ended without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The COLLEGE Act would require colleges with large endowments to pay a share of each full-time student's cost of attendance — 25% at schools with endowments over $1 billion, 50% at $5 billion, and 75% at $10 billion or more. It would also make every college in the federal loan program pay a growing share of the loan balances of its students who default, rising from 1% to 25% over 25 years. And it would force colleges to publicly report, by major, graduation rates, graduate wages, costs, and debt.
analysis.who_benefits: Students and their families at expensive colleges, who would see a quarter to three-quarters of their cost of attendance picked up by the school if it has a billion-dollar endowment. Student borrowers generally benefit because colleges would have to pay part of the loan balances of students who default, giving schools a financial reason to keep students from failing. Students choosing a college would gain from required public data on wages, debt, and graduation rates by major. Taxpayers also benefit, since loan defaults currently come largely out of federal funds.

how_it_helps.text: Colleges with endowments over $1 billion would have to pay 25% of each full-time student's cost of attendance, and the share rises to 50% at $5 billion and 75% at $10 billion — directly lowering what enrolled students pay.

Every college in the federal direct loan program would remit a risk-sharing payment based on the loan balances of its students who default, starting at 1% and rising to 25% of that balance over 25 years, so schools share the cost when their graduates cannot repay.

Colleges would have to report — and the Education Department would have to publish — per-major data on 4-year graduation rates, employment, median wages 1, 3, and 5 years after graduation, cost to graduate, and average debt and default rates, letting students compare programs before enrolling.
Colleges would have to explain each year any increase in the cost of attendance and disclose endowment size and growth, making tuition hikes and endowment gains visible to the public.

analysis.who_pays: Wealthy universities with endowments over $1 billion would pay the largest direct cost — up to 75% of every full-time student's cost of attendance. All colleges participating in federal loans would bear risk-sharing payments tied to student defaults, hitting hardest the schools whose graduates default most, such as for-profit colleges. Some schools might try to pass costs on through higher tuition, reduced aid, or tighter admissions, which would fall back on students.

drawbacks.text: The cost-match mandate is blunt: paying 25% to 75% of the full cost of attendance for every full-time student is an enormous sum for even the richest schools, and colleges might respond by shrinking enrollment, cutting other aid, or raising charges — shifting some of the burden back onto students.

The default risk-sharing penalty falls on schools for outcomes they only partly control, and could pressure community colleges and other open-access institutions that serve low-income students to admit fewer of the very students the aid system is meant for.
The detailed reporting requirements apply to every college in the federal aid programs, adding administrative costs that small institutions would feel most.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The goals — making wealthy schools share costs, giving colleges a financial stake in whether their graduates can repay loans, and publishing wage-and-debt data by major — are ones most students and taxpayers would welcome, and versions of risk-sharing and program-level disclosure have broad appeal. But this bill's design is heavy-handed: the cost-match percentages are set at levels few institutions could absorb without changing behavior in ways that could hurt students, and the escalating default penalty could penalize schools for serving high-risk populations. It was also a single-sponsor bill with no cosponsors and no committee work, so it was never refined through the process where such problems normally get fixed.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in August 2022 and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors until the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Rick Scott of Florida introduced the COLLEGE Act on August 4, 2022.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action was ever taken: the bill drew no cosponsors and received no committee hearing or floor vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wealthy universities with billion-dollar endowments are better off, because they were never required to cover a share of their students' costs, and no college ever had to pay default risk-sharing fees. Students and taxpayers gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never came to a vote, so no one's position was tested on the record; it had a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.industry: Wealthy universities with endowments over $1 billion
industries.note: These schools would have had to pay 25% to 75% of every full-time student's cost of attendance, drawing directly on billion-dollar endowments. The bill died, so their endowments and pricing power remain untouched.

The risk-sharing provision would have made colleges pay a share of the loan balances of students who default, and schools whose graduates default most — disproportionately for-profit institutions — would have paid the most. Their interest was in keeping defaults costless to them.

All colleges in the federal loan program would have faced a new default fee and extensive per-major reporting requirements. The transparency would help students choose, but the compliance costs and default penalties cut against the sector.
